opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'm excited about video generation because I don't really see it as a media tool. I see it as a step toward world models.

When you train a model to generate realistic video, you're forcing it to learn a lot about how the world works. Objects have permanence. Liquids splash. Light reflects off surfaces. If you push a glass off a table, it falls and shatters. No one hand-codes any of that into the model. It picks up an intuitive physics engine just from watching enormous amounts of video. It isn't perfect, and you still see artifacts like hands merging or objects popping in and out. But the trend line is very clear.

For me, coming from robotics and embodied AI, this matters a lot. The biggest bottleneck in robotics is data. We have the whole internet for language models, but no "internet of robot actions." Real-world robot data is slow, expensive, and hard to scale. Traditional physics simulators help a lot, but building those environments still takes heavy manual work from graphics artists and engineers.

Video generation models could become a kind of neural simulator, or what I sometimes call a data-driven simulation of the world. You can imagine prompting a model to generate thousands of variations of a kitchen, with different lighting, objects, and layouts, and then training robot policies inside those imagined worlds. Eventually you'd make them interactive, so the model responds to actions and isn't just producing passive video.

So the creative uses are amazing, for filmmakers and artists, but the deeper story is that video models are learning to simulate reality. Once you can simulate reality, you can train agents that act in it. That's the bridge from pixels to physical intelligence, and I think it's one of the most important threads in AI right now.

r001.rationale: The response describes video generation models as a “neural simulator” and says they learn to simulate reality.

r002.rationale: It says the model picks up an intuitive physics engine from watching video, with no hand-coded physics.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The reason I'm excited about video generation has very little to do with making pretty clips, and everything to do with robotics.

If you think about what a video model actually has to learn in order to generate a coherent sequence of frames, it has to learn an enormous amount about how the physical world works. Objects have to persist when they go behind something. Liquids have to pour, cloth has to drape, a hand has to deform a sponge in a plausible way. Light has to behave consistently as the camera moves. Nobody writes those rules down. The model absorbs them from watching an incredible amount of video, which is by far the largest and richest source of data about physical reality we have. Text can describe the world, but video shows it.

So what you end up with is, essentially, a learned simulator. A world model. And that's the thing robotics has been missing. In language we had the internet, trillions of tokens, and that's what made scaling work. In robotics we have nothing like that. Collecting real robot data is slow, expensive, and you break hardware. Hand-built simulators are great for rigid bodies but they're terrible at the messy stuff like food, fabric, fluids, and everything that actually matters in a kitchen or a home.

A video model that understands physics gives you a way around that bottleneck. You can ask it, "here's a robot, here's a scene, what happens if it moves its arm this way?" and it dreams the outcome. You can generate millions of diverse scenarios, lighting conditions, object layouts, that would be impossible to build by hand. And in the limit, the model that predicts video and the model that plans actions start to become the same model. Predicting the next frame and predicting the next motor command are really two views of the same problem: understanding what happens next in the world.

That's the bet I'm excited about. Video generation is how we scale physical intelligence the way we scaled language.

r001.rationale: The response calls a video model “essentially, a learned simulator” and “a world model.”

r002.rationale: It says the model absorbs physical rules from watching video and that nobody writes those rules down, conveying physics learned from data rather than hand-written rules.

astra-6.text:
What excites me most is that video generation could be a path toward building world models. To generate a convincing video, a model has to learn something about how the world works—how objects move, how they interact, and what happens next. It’s not necessarily learning the physics correctly, but there’s a lot more going on than making individual images look good.

For robotics, that’s a really exciting possibility. Imagine a model that can take an action and predict its consequences visually. A robot could use that to explore possible futures before acting in the real world. We’re not there just because we can generate beautiful videos, but the potential connection between video generation, simulation, and learning to act is what really excites me.

r001.rationale: It presents video generation as learning how the world works and visually predicting what follows from actions, linking it to simulation.

r002.rationale: It says the model may not learn physics correctly and does not claim that models learn physics from data alone.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me most is the possibility that video generation becomes a way to simulate the world. To generate a convincing video, a model has to learn something about how objects move, how they interact, and what happens over time. That could be incredibly useful for robotics, where collecting real-world experience is slow and expensive.

Imagine a robot being able to explore many possible outcomes before taking an action. If I push this object, will it slide or tip over? If I reach around this obstacle, can I grasp what’s behind it? A sufficiently capable video model could help predict those outcomes.

The big question is whether it learns reliable physics or just produces something that looks plausible. Those are different standards. But the possibility of turning video generation into a useful world model—that’s what I find really exciting.

r001.rationale: It describes video generation as a way to simulate the world and predict outcomes.

r002.rationale: It says models may learn how objects move and interact, but does not claim they learn physics from data alone.
